title: Whose Answers Count for the County? — Gelman & Little (1997) Multilevel Regression and Poststratification (MRP), Census Demographic Cell Weighting & Zhang County-Level COPD Surveillance Validation

teenKit.tldr: In 15 seconds: National health surveys rarely interview enough people in small rural counties to trust raw percentages, and volunteers don't match the local census. Multilevel Regression and Poststratification (MRP) borrows strength across demographics and reweights every cell to the true county population.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Public-health departments need accurate county maps for asthma, COPD, and screening—without falling for noisy 12-person subsamples or nonresponse bias.
keyTakeaways: Multilevel regression estimates outcome probabilities for detailed demographic-by-geography cells using partial pooling so small cells shrink sensibly toward group patterns.
Poststratification multiplies each cell's predicted probability by the exact U.S. Census headcount in that county and sums them up.
Zhang et al. validated CDC county-level MRP chronic-disease estimates against direct local surveys, showing dramatic gains over raw sample proportions.

vocab.meaning: Hierarchical shrinkage that blends noisy small-group data with broader population patterns according to sample precision.
Weighting model predictions for each demographic cell by known population census counts so unrepresentative survey samples match the real community.

quiz.question: What are the two core stages of Gelman and Little's MRP?
options: Random dialing followed by p-value pruning
Fitting a hierarchical model across demographic-geographic cells, then weighting cell predictions by true Census population counts
Deleting counties with fewer than 1,000 residents
Averaging national totals equally across all counties
quiz.explanation: Multilevel modeling stabilizes sparse cell estimates, and Census poststratification corrects sample demographic imbalance.
